title: Task-Optimized Convolutional Recurrent Networks Align with Tactile Process

predicted_errors.error_location: Section 4, “Importance of Architectural Inductive Bias” versus Appendix A5, Table 7
predicted_errors.supporting_evidence: The Results state that “All trained EAD models outperformed raw sensor inputs in neural alignment,” and immediately report that the raw input achieves RSA correlation 0.46. However, Table 7 reports a trained “Inter+SimCLR with Temporal Masking” model with neural fit 0.42, which is below 0.46. Thus the universal claim that all trained models outperform raw input is false.

predicted_errors.error_location: Figure 4 caption and Appendix A4, “Inter-Animal Consistency”
predicted_errors.supporting_evidence: Figure 4 states that the maximum pairwise animal-to-animal score is 0.34. Appendix A4 instead reports: “The mean pooled animal score was 0.175 with a s.e.m. of 0.161 and maximum score of 1.34.” Both are presented as inter-animal neural-consistency quantities. A maximum of 1.34 directly conflicts with the figure’s stated maximum of 0.34 unless they are distinct metrics, but the paper does not define such a distinction.

The appendix calls the quantity a correlation/RSA score and reports a “maximum score of 1.34.” A Pearson correlation cannot exceed 1. If this is a noise-corrected estimator that can exceed one because of sampling error or denominator correction, it must not be reported or interpreted as a Pearson r/noise ceiling without explicitly explaining its unbounded behavior. Elsewhere the paper repeatedly labels these values “RSA Pearson’s r.”

predicted_errors.error_location: Methods, “Neural Data Comparison,” and Results claims of neural-fit saturation
predicted_errors.supporting_evidence: Neural RSA is evaluated on only six stimulus conditions (concave/convex at three distances), hence an RDM has only 15 off-diagonal entries. The paper then reports, for every model, “the maximum, across all layers” of neural alignment using those same six conditions. No held-out stimuli or independent layer-selection set is used. Selecting the best layer on the neural evaluation data inflates reported fit, and the six stimuli cannot support the claim that models “saturated all of the held-out explainable neural variance”; no held-out neural stimulus evaluation is described.

predicted_errors.error_location: Section 4, “ConvRNN Encoders Saturate Explainable Neural Variance in Rodent Somatosensory Cortex”
predicted_errors.supporting_evidence: The paper asserts that the best models “saturated all of the held-out explainable neural variance,” “robustly pass[ed] the NeuroAI Turing Test,” and support essential recurrent processing. These conclusions are substantially stronger than the described evidence: the neural comparison has only six conditions, uses maximization over layers on the same neural data, and has internally inconsistent inter-animal ceilings (0.34 versus 1.34). The evidence therefore cannot establish saturation or a robust benchmark pass.

predicted_errors.error_location: Figure 5(a) caption/legend versus Methods, “Model Training and Tactile Augmentations”
predicted_errors.supporting_evidence: Figure 5(a) labels the SSL losses as “SimCLR,” “SwAV,” and “AE.” The Methods describe the SSL objectives as SimCLR, SimSiam, and AE, with no SwAV method, training protocol, or result described anywhere. Thus the figure either mislabels SimSiam as SwAV or reports an unreported method.

predicted_errors.error_location: Appendix Figure A1 legend versus Methods and Tables 3–5
predicted_errors.supporting_evidence: Figure A1’s legend lists attenders “cnn, gpt, llama, none” and losses including “vicreg.” The stated experimental search instead uses None, GPT, and Mamba attenders, and supervised/SimCLR/SimSiam/AE objectives. Neither Llama nor VICReg is defined or trained in the methods, while Mamba and SimSiam are absent from this figure legend. This makes the plotted results uninterpretable as results from the reported experiment.

predicted_errors.error_location: Abstract, Introduction, and Results statements comparing ConvRNNs with S4
predicted_errors.supporting_evidence: The paper repeatedly claims ConvRNNs are superior to S4/SSM encoders for categorization and neural alignment. Yet Figure 3 explicitly says “Models with the encoder being S4 are excluded as the training losses explode before the first epoch is finished.” A failed, excluded training run does not provide a task-performance comparison supporting superiority. The paper should describe S4 as failing under the tested optimization setup, not as a demonstrated inferior architecture.

predicted_errors.error_location: Introduction, paragraph discussing robotic whisker sensors: citation to Simon et al. [2023]
predicted_errors.supporting_evidence: The text cites Simon et al. [2023] for the claim that bio-inspired whisker sensors cannot discriminate simultaneous airflow, direct-contact, and inertia stimuli. The cited reference is “FlowDrone: Wind estimation and gust rejection on UAVs using fast-response hot-wire flow sensors,” which concerns UAV hot-wire wind sensing, not whisker-array sensors or simultaneous contact/inertia discrimination. It does not support the stated claim.

predicted_errors.error_location: Introduction, paragraph discussing magnetic tactile sensors: citation to Bhirangi et al. [2024b]
predicted_errors.supporting_evidence: The manuscript cites Bhirangi et al. [2024b] for claims that magnetic tactile sensors have low spatial resolution and electromagnetic-interference errors. But the reference entry for Bhirangi et al. [2024b] is “Hierarchical state space models for continuous sequence-to-sequence modeling,” which is unrelated to magnetic tactile sensing or electromagnetic interference.

predicted_errors.error_location: Introduction, first paragraph: citation to Sterbing-D’Angelo et al. [2011]
predicted_errors.supporting_evidence: The text says “specialized insect hairs respond to wind stimuli” and cites Sterbing-D’Angelo et al. [2011]. The cited paper is titled “Bat wing sensors support flight control,” not a study of insect hairs. The citation is misattributed and does not support the stated example.

predicted_errors.error_location: Appendix A5, Table 6 and its decoding protocol
predicted_errors.supporting_evidence: Table 6 says that for each of six stimuli, a logistic-regression decoder is trained on the other five and tested on the held-out one. If there is one representation per condition as described, aggregate leave-one-condition-out accuracy across six held-out conditions must occur in increments of 1/6 (e.g., 0.50, 0.667), not reported values such as 0.56, 0.58, or 0.54. The paper supplies no repeated samples, resampling, or averaging protocol for model scores that could produce these values. The reported decoding numbers therefore do not follow from the stated evaluation design.

The paper says temporal masking improved top-5 accuracy “slightly (~5%).” The displayed changes are 0.15 to 0.18 and 0.23 to 0.28. These are respectively 3 and 5 percentage points, but approximately 20% and 22% relative increases—not approximately 5% under a percent-improvement interpretation. The magnitude must be stated consistently.
